svg.title: Half the gland or all of it: the line at 2 cm and what each side costs
svg.desc: A schematic in six parts about how much thyroid to remove in differentiated thyroid cancer. The first part is the line itself, in three cards side by side, following recommendations 15A, 15B and 15C of the 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines. Recommendation 15A: for a tumour of 2 cm or smaller (cT1) with no gross extrathyroidal extension and no clinical nodal or distant metastasis, the initial operation "should be" a thyroid lobectomy - a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence - unless there is cancer on both sides or another reason the contralateral lobe must come out; the verb in this cell is not "may" but "should". Recommendation 15B: for tumours above 2 cm and up to 4 cm, lobectomy "may be the preferred" initial treatment, a conditional recommendation with low-to-moderate certainty, on the grounds that the risks and side effects are clearly lower, though the patient and team may also choose total thyroidectomy to allow radioiodine or to make follow-up easier to read. Recommendation 15C: for tumours larger than 4 cm, any size with gross extrathyroidal extension, clinically apparent nodal metastasis, or distant metastasis already present, the initial operation should include total thyroidectomy, a strong recommendation with moderate certainty. A panel beneath sets this against recommendation 35B of the 2015 edition: for tumours larger than 1 cm and smaller than 4 cm without extrathyroidal extension and without clinical nodal metastasis, the initial operation could be bilateral or unilateral, and for low-risk papillary and follicular carcinoma a lobectomy "may be sufficient", a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. The operative word was "may"; in the cell at or below 2 cm the 2025 edition replaced it with "should". The second part is a crossed-out box reading "a trial that randomises lobectomy against total thyroidectomy": the only registered randomised attempt was a feasibility pilot at one American centre whose primary endpoint was the proportion of eligible patients willing to enrol, with 2 an actual enrolment count of 2 according to the registry, closing in January 2026, the registry entry giving the number enrolled and no separate number randomised. Beside it, the 2025 guidelines are quoted as saying that because outcomes in low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer are generally good and randomised controlled trials are lacking, the committee had to rely on large database studies. The third part is the databases, drawn as intervals on a logarithmic axis with a dashed line marked "1 = no difference". The three intervals come from the 2014 re-analysis of the American cancer database (61,775 papillary carcinomas of 1.0 to 4.0 cm diagnosed 1998 to 2006, median follow-up 82 months, adjusted overall survival): all tumours 1.0 to 4.0 cm, hazard ratio 0.96 (95% confidence interval 0.84 to 1.09); 1.0 to 2.0 cm, 1.05 (0.88 to 1.26); 2.1 to 4.0 cm, 0.89 (0.73 to 1.07). All three sit close to 1, and a 2015 paper on stage I patients under 45 with tumours of 1.1 to 4.0 cm found the same. The same panel records the 2007 analysis of 52,173 papillary carcinomas, in which the extent of surgery affected neither recurrence nor survival below 1 cm, while above 1 cm lobectomy carried a higher risk of recurrence and of death, including in the 1 to 2 cm cell taken alone. Three caveats follow: the endpoint is overall survival rather than disease-specific survival, and most people with differentiated thyroid cancer die of something else; the two groups were never the same people, since in the 2014 paper nodal metastasis was 27% against 7%, extrathyroidal extension 16% against 5% and multifocal disease 44% against 29%, which is confounding by indication; and the "stage I" of the 2015 paper uses the AJCC seventh edition cut-off of 45 years rather than the eighth edition's 55. The fourth part is whether the tablet is needed after half the gland. Two cards side by side: with the target set at the normal reference range, roughly seven to eight in ten people need no thyroxine after a lobectomy; with the target set at the older, lower range, only two to three in ten. The 2025 edition says that for people whose recurrence risk falls in the low or moderate cells, using the older three-tier wording, the TSH target is the normal reference range whether the operation was total thyroidectomy or lobectomy. A panel below is headed "every cohort below used the old target as its threshold" and carries three bars: TSH above 2 mIU/L within one year, 73% (350 of the 478 patients not already on thyroxine, within a cohort of 555 lobectomies); thyroxine used after lobectomy for malignancy, 59.3% (of 33,756 lobectomies in a national claims dataset, against 39.4% of those done for benign disease, adjusted odds ratio 2.34, 95% confidence interval 2.20 to 2.48, with that dataset not recording where each target was set); and diagnosed hypothyroid after lobectomy, 22% (a 2012 meta-analysis of 32 studies, 95% confidence interval 19 to 27, with only 4 studies separating clinical from subclinical disease at 12% and 4%, mixing benign with malignant, its endpoint being diagnosed hypothyroid rather than taking a tablet, and with the 2025 guidelines labelling that 22% as biochemical where the original does not - what is drawn is the original). Below that, who is more likely to be found hypothyroid afterwards: a preoperative TSH above 2.5, relative risk 3.16 (2.03 to 4.90); positive thyroid antibodies 3.52; thyroiditis on the pathology 3.30 - all with the endpoint of being diagnosed hypothyroid rather than starting thyroxine. The fifth part is completion thyroidectomy: retrospective studies 5% to 43%, meta-analyses 11% to 34%, conversion to total thyroidectomy during the operation for high-risk features about 21%, and completion thyroidectomy on the final pathology about 27% to 30%. The 2025 edition writes one sentence patients are to be told in advance: there is at least a one-in-five chance of conversion during the operation or completion afterwards. Two figures describe the second operation: in a single-institution cohort of 786 people, the 149 who had lobectomy followed by completion thyroidectomy had less transient hypoparathyroidism than the 637 who had a total thyroidectomy in one sitting; and in a national surgical quality registry of 70,638 people, 30-day mortality was 0.1% for both with comparable overall complications, though that registry does not capture hypoparathyroidism or recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. The sixth part sets the two sides against each other in two cards separated by a dashed rule. Total thyroidectomy against lobectomy, as relative risks from meta-analysis: transient hypocalcaemia close to tenfold, permanent hypocalcaemia about threefold, and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and postoperative bleeding both between one point seven and two point six; the figure deliberately gives no absolute percentages, because those depend on how the hospital examines the larynx and on how many months count as permanent. The lobectomy side: a second operation is possible; recurrence after lobectomy mostly appears in the contralateral lobe and can usually be retrieved by completion thyroidectomy; in a 30-year Japanese cohort 18 of 1,327 patients (1.4%) who had a lobectomy for low-risk papillary microcarcinoma recurred in the remaining thyroid; and follow-up is not lighter, only different. The figure ends with a red-framed panel of readings that are barred: "taking it all out is cleaner" is not what this line rests on; the database papers measure overall survival and the two groups were never the same people, so no difference seen is not a difference disproved; "half the gland means no tablet" depends on where the target is set; what a lobectomy spares is not a lifetime of tablets but the replacement that is inevitable after the whole gland comes out; and the figure is not a tool for deciding your own extent of surgery - whether to operate at all is in "Watching instead of operating, on conditions", the nodes in "Should the nodes come out too", the denominators and definitions of the complications in "What the operation takes with it", and the dose in "The tablet you take for life, and how much". At the foot are five questions to read out at the clinic: how many centimetres does mine measure and is it in the cell at or below 2 cm; do you think I will need radioiodine and if so does the whole gland have to come out; if the frozen section or final pathology shows high-risk features would you recommend completion thyroidectomy and roughly what is the chance; if I have a lobectomy when will you check my TSH and above what value would you start me on thyroxine; and if I choose the lobectomy, what am I giving up.

g.text: HALF THE GLAND OR ALL OF IT - WHERE THE
LINE SITS, AND WHAT EACH SIDE COSTS
The line sits at 2 cm, and
the verb has changed
from "may" to "should"
The 2015 edition said that between 1 and 4 cm a
lobectomy "may" be enough. The 2025 edition splits
that cell in two, and in the part at or below 2 cm the
verb is "should", as a strong recommendation with
moderate certainty.
There is no randomised trial underneath this line.
What each side of it costs, and what "half the gland
means no tablet" really looks like, are both on this
figure.
One - the 2025 edition splits this cell into
three
American Thyroid Association 2025, recommendations 15A, 15B and 15C.
The size of the tumour is measured, not sensed.
Rec 15A - cT1, up to 2 cm, N0M0
Tumour 2 cm or smaller, no gross extrathyroidal
extension, no clinical nodal or distant metastasis
The initial operation "should be" a thyroid
lobectomy
Strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence
Unless there is cancer on both sides, or another reason the
contralateral lobe must come out. The verb in this cell is not "may";
it is "should".
Rec 15B - above 2 cm to 4 cm
Again with no gross extrathyroidal extension and no
clinical nodal or distant metastasis
Lobectomy "may be the preferred" initial
treatment
Conditional recommendation, low-to-moderate certainty
The reason given is that the risks and side effects are clearly lower;
but the patient and the treating team may also choose total
thyroidectomy, to allow radioiodine or to make follow-up easier to
read.
Rec 15C - the other side of the line
Tumour larger than 4 cm; any size with gross
extrathyroidal extension; clinically apparent nodal
metastasis; or distant metastasis already present
The initial operation should include total
thyroidectomy
Strong recommendation, moderate certainty
This cell is not part of the half-or-all question at all.
What recommendation 35B of the 2015 edition looked like
For tumours larger than 1 cm and smaller than 4 cm, without
extrathyroidal extension and without clinical nodal metastasis, the
initial operation could be bilateral or unilateral; for low-risk papillary
and follicular carcinoma a lobectomy "may be sufficient". Strong
recommendation, moderate-quality evidence.
The operative word was "may". In the cell at or below 2 cm, the 2025
edition replaced it with "should".
Two - there is no randomised trial
underneath this line
A trial that randomises lobectomy against total thyroidectomy
The only registered randomised attempt was a feasibility pilot at one
American centre. Its primary endpoint was the proportion of eligible
patients willing to enrol - that is, a test of whether a formal trial would be
feasible at all. The registry gives an actual enrolment count of 2, and the
study closed in January 2026; the registry entry gives the number
enrolled and no separate number randomised.
The 2025 guidelines say it themselves: because outcomes in low-risk
differentiated thyroid cancer are generally good and randomised
controlled trials are lacking, the committee considered that it had to
rely on large database studies. The shape of the evidence decides
how every number below should be read.
Three - what the databases said, and what
they did not
The 2014 re-analysis of the American cancer database: 61,775 papillary
carcinomas of 1.0 to 4.0 cm diagnosed between 1998 and 2006, median
follow-up 82 months. After adjustment, no difference in overall survival
between the two operations.
All tumours 1.0 to 4.0 cm
Hazard ratio 0.96 (95% confidence interval 0.84 to 1.09)
1.0 to 2.0 cm
Hazard ratio 1.05 (0.88 to 1.26)
2.1 to 4.0 cm
Hazard ratio 0.89 (0.73 to 1.07)
1 = no difference
All three intervals sit close to 1. A 2015 paper looking at stage I
patients under 45 with tumours of 1.1 to 4.0 cm found the same.
The 2007 analysis of the same database, covering 52,173 papillary
carcinomas, is the classic statement of the old idea that anything above 1 cm
needs a total thyroidectomy: below 1 cm the extent of surgery affected
neither recurrence nor survival; above 1 cm, lobectomy carried a higher
risk of recurrence and of death, including in the 1 to 2 cm cell taken on its
own.
But two things have to be said alongside these
The endpoint is not the one you assume
Their endpoint is overall survival, not disease-specific survival.
Most people with differentiated thyroid cancer die of something else,
so overall survival is heavily diluted.
The two groups were never the same people
In the 2014 paper, 27% of those who had a total thyroidectomy had
nodal metastasis against 7% of the lobectomy group; extrathyroidal
extension 16% against 5%; multifocal disease 44% against 29%.
Surgeons were already sending the more threatening-looking
disease for total thyroidectomy. This is confounding by indication,
and no database is large enough to make it go away.
And there is a versioning problem
The "stage I" in the 2015 paper uses the AJCC seventh edition cut-off
of 45 years, not the eighth edition's 55, so it cannot be laid against a
report written today.
Four - whether you need the tablet after
half the gland depends on where the target
is set
The 2025 edition says that for people whose recurrence risk falls in the
low or moderate cells (using the older three-tier wording), the TSH target
is the normal reference range whether the operation was a total
thyroidectomy or a lobectomy.
Target = the normal reference range
Proportion needing no thyroxine after lobectomy
Seven to eight in ten
The 2025 guidelines, reporting earlier studies: with the target set at
the normal reference range, roughly seven to eight in ten people
who have a lobectomy need no thyroxine supplementation.
TSH is the signal the pituitary sends to tell the thyroid to work.
Target = the old, lower range
The same thing, measured against a different line
Two to three in ten
With the target set at the older, lower range, only two to three in ten
need no supplementation. So "do I have to take it" is really the
question "where has your target been set".
The same people, a different threshold, two very different answers.
Every cohort below used the old target as its
threshold
So what they answer is "how many fell short of the old target", not
"how many have no choice but to take thyroxine after a lobectomy".
TSH above 2 mIU/L within one year
Thyroxine used after lobectomy for malignancy
Diagnosed hypothyroid after lobectomy
73%: in a cohort of 555 lobectomies, 350 of the 478 who were not on
thyroxine beforehand had a TSH above 2 mIU/L within one year. The
threshold is the old target line of TSH 2 mIU/L.
59.3%: among 33,756 lobectomies in a national claims dataset, 59.3% of those
operated on for malignancy used thyroxine, against 39.4% of those operated
on for benign disease, adjusted odds ratio 2.34 (95% confidence interval 2.20
to 2.48). That dataset does not tell us where each of those targets was set.
22%: a 2012 meta-analysis of 32 studies found an overall risk of
hypothyroidism after lobectomy of 22% (95% confidence interval 19 to 27);
only 4 of those studies separated clinical from subclinical disease,
estimating 12% subclinical and 4% clinical. That figure mixes benign with
malignant, and its endpoint is being diagnosed hypothyroid, not taking a
tablet. The 2025 guidelines label that 22% as biochemical, which the original
does not; what is drawn here is the original.
Who is more likely to be found hypothyroid after the operation
A preoperative TSH above 2.5: relative risk 3.16 (2.03 to 4.90).
Positive thyroid antibodies: 3.52.
Thyroiditis on the pathology: 3.30.
The endpoint of that set is being diagnosed hypothyroid, not starting
thyroxine. A relative risk divides the proportion in one group by the
proportion in another, which is a different calculation from the
hazard ratio above, that looks at the rate at which things happen.
Five - completion thyroidectomy: how
many get there, and what it costs
Retrospective studies
Meta-analyses
Converted to total thyroidectomy during the operation for high-risk
features
About 21%
Completion thyroidectomy on the final pathology
About 27% to 30%
The 2025 edition writes one sentence that patients are to be told in
advance
There is at least a one-in-five chance of conversion to total
thyroidectomy during the operation, or of completion thyroidectomy
afterwards. Choosing a lobectomy means knowing in advance that a
second operation is possible.
In a single-institution cohort of 786 people, the 149 who had a
lobectomy followed by completion thyroidectomy had less
transient hypoparathyroidism than the 637 who had a total
thyroidectomy in one sitting.
In a national surgical quality registry of 70,638 people, 30-day
mortality was 0.1% for both and overall complications were
comparable; but that registry does not capture
hypoparathyroidism or recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, so the
"safety" it reports cannot be used to talk about the voice or blood
calcium.
Six - what each side costs
Total thyroidectomy against lobectomy
Relative risks from meta-analysis: transient hypocalcaemia close
to tenfold.
Permanent hypocalcaemia about threefold.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and postoperative bleeding both
between one point seven and two point six.
This figure deliberately gives no absolute percentages: those
depend on how the hospital examines the larynx and on how many
months count as permanent. The denominator and definition of
every one of them is in "What the operation takes with it".
The lobectomy side
A second operation is possible - the ranges in the section above.
The 2025 edition says recurrence after lobectomy mostly
appears in the contralateral lobe, and can usually be retrieved by
completion thyroidectomy.
In a 30-year Japanese cohort, 18 of 1,327 patients (1.4%) who had
a lobectomy for low-risk papillary microcarcinoma had a
recurrence in the remaining thyroid.
Follow-up is not lighter, it is different: with half a thyroid still
there, the baseline against which thyroglobulin is read is not the
one used after a total thyroidectomy.
What this figure must not be read to say
"Taking it all out is cleaner" is not what this line rests on. In
the cell at or below 2 cm the guideline says the initial
operation should be a lobectomy, as a strong
recommendation with moderate certainty.
The endpoint of those database papers is overall survival,
not disease-specific survival, and the two groups were
never the same people (nodal metastasis 27% against 7%,
extrathyroidal extension 16% against 5%, multifocal disease
44% against 29%). No difference seen is not the same as a
difference disproved.
"Half the gland means no tablet" depends on where the
target is set: roughly seven to eight in ten need no
supplementation when the target is the normal reference
range, against two to three in ten under the old lower target,
and every cohort below used that old line.
What a lobectomy can spare is not "a lifetime of tablets" but
the replacement that is inevitable after the whole gland
comes out.
And this figure is not a tool for deciding your own extent of
surgery. Whether to operate at all is in "Watching instead of
operating, on conditions"; whether the nodes come out is in
"Should the nodes come out too"; the denominators and
definitions of the complications are in "What the operation
takes with it"; and how much thyroxine is in "The tablet you
take for life, and how much".
How much to take out: who to ask, and what
How many centimetres does mine measure? Is it in the cell
at or below 2 cm?
Do you think I will need radioiodine? If I do, does that mean
the whole gland has to come out?
If the frozen section or the final pathology shows high-risk
features, would you recommend completion
thyroidectomy? Roughly what is the chance of that?
If I have a lobectomy, when will you check my TSH? Above
what value would you start me on thyroxine?
If I choose the lobectomy, what am I giving up?
Schematic, redrawn from the 2025 and 2015 American Thyroid
Association guidelines, the two analyses of the American cancer
database, a national claims dataset, two meta-analyses of
hypothyroidism after lobectomy and two completion-thyroidectomy
cohorts; not reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The
cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the
data points must not be compared directly.
